name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
title: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
answer: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of turning an organization's completed projects, publications, reports, and prior applications into new grant proposal text. It includes finding reusable claims, evidence, and project descriptions, then adapting them to a new funder's questions and format. The goal is to reduce repetitive writing while keeping the proposal specific to the new opportunity. On this site, the library of 135 research papers and 11222 extracted claims shows the kind of source material that can be mined for such drafts.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of turning an organization's completed projects, publications, reports, and prior applications into new grant proposal text. It includes finding reusable claims, evidence, and project descriptions, then adapting them to a new funder's questions and format. The goal is to reduce repetitive writing while keeping the proposal specific to the new opportunity. On this site, the library of 135 research papers and 11222 extracted claims shows the kind of source material that can be mined for such drafts.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a searchable archive of past documents, usually with extracted text and metadata such as project dates, funders, and outcomes. A retrieval step pulls relevant passages, and a language model or drafting assistant turns them into proposal sections. The system needs access controls so that only authorized staff can see confidential past applications. It also needs a way to keep source links attached to each reused passage.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners first identify the new funder's requirements and map them to past work that addresses similar goals. They then retrieve claims and evidence from the archive, often using the 11222 extracted claims as a model for how to break long documents into reusable statements. A draft is generated section by section, with placeholders for budget figures, timelines, and partner names that must be checked by hand. Each generated sentence is reviewed against the source before it is accepted.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are self-plagiarism, reuse of outdated or inaccurate results, and accidental disclosure of confidential information from past proposals. Provenance matters: every reused claim should point back to the original paper or report, and this site links to the original paper rather than to a secondary search tool. Organizations need clear rules about who may reuse which documents and whether funders require disclosure of prior related work. Human review and sign-off remain necessary before submission.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward claim-level libraries that store reusable findings with their source, context, and limitations attached. Future systems may compare a draft against funder scoring criteria and flag weak or unsupported statements. Audit trails that show exactly which past document each sentence came from are likely to become standard. Over time, proposal drafting may become a review and editing task rather than a writing task.
